L171: A member this document does not define for a type MUST be refused. This departs from the in-toto parsing rule that consumers ignore unknown fields: a revision that adds a member publishes it under a new predicate type URI (【120†Section 9】), so a reader of a v1 type never meets a member it has not been told how to read.【121†¶】
L172: 
L173: Each `subject` member carries a `digest` holding only `sha256`. What the digest is taken over is stated for each type.【122†¶】
L174: ### 【33†4.2.】 【34†Common predicate members】
L175: 
L176: Every predicate defined here carries these members:【123†¶】
L177: 
L178: incident:
L179: 
L180: 
L181: An object with `issuer`, an https URL naming who assigns the identifier; `id`, a non-empty string; and, optionally, `related`, a list of further `{issuer, id}` pairs naming the same incident in another organization's records. This is the term `incident_identifier` of [【110†VOCABULARY】].【124†¶】
L182: 
L183: 
L184: producer:
L185: 
L186: 
L187: An object with `id`, an https URL naming the signing party.【125†¶】
L188: 
L189: issuedAt:
L190: 
L191: 
L192: The time the record was issued.【126†¶】
L193: 
L194: 
L195: registryDigest:
L196: 
L197: 
L198: An object with `sha256`, the SHA-256 of the exact bytes of the [【110†VOCABULARY】] registry the record's closed values are expressed in.【127†¶】
L199: 
L200: 
L201: doesNotAssert:
L202: 
L203: 
L204: A list of non-empty strings, each stating something the producer says the record does not claim. The list MAY be empty; the member MUST NOT be absent.【128†¶】
L205: Where a type uses it, `predecessors` is a list of `{predicateType, digest}` naming earlier records of this document, where `digest` holds the `sha256` of the predecessor statement's bytes exactly as carried in its DSSE payload.【129†¶】
L206: ### 【35†4.3.】 【36†Closed values】
L207: The values of `response_function`, `pause_hold`, `restoration_decision`, `revocation_state`, `intent_binding`, `independence_basis` and `set_sufficiency` are those of the registry whose digest is `1c5ff80bd97237a603afc402db692ffe5abe15e4a7f9eca13f20068ada347fdc`, published under https://w3id.org/agent-evidence/vocab/v1/registry/ with the file name `sha256-`, then the digest, then `.yaml`. Values that a section of this document lists itself are closed by this document.【130†¶】
L208: A reader MUST refuse a value outside a closed set and MUST NOT ignore the member. Registration in [【110†VOCABULARY】] gives a value its identity; which values a member accepts is set by this document alone.【131†¶】
L209: ### 【37†4.4.】 【38†Rule order and verdicts】
L210: 
L211: Each type has an ordered rule table. A reader applies the rules in order and reports the first that fails, with its reason code. Rules 1 to 3 are the same for every type:【132†¶】
L212: 【133†Table 1】
L213: #  | Rule  | Code
L214: --- | --- | ---
L215: 1  | The statement has the shape of 【134†Section 4.1】 and the predicate type of this section  | `statement-malformed`
L216: 2  | The predicate has exactly its members, each well formed  | `predicate-malformed`
L217: 3  | Every closed value is in its set  | `closed-vocabulary-violation`
L218: A record that passes every rule of its type is accepted with the verdict named for the type. Two readers that apply this document reach the same verdict and the same first failing reason on the same bytes; the conformance corpus (【135†Section 10】) tests that.【136†¶】
L219: ## 【39†5.】 【40†Record Types】
L220: The five predicate type URIs are:【137†¶】
L221: 
L222:     https://probityai.github.io/agent-evidence-vectors/predicate/v1/
L223:       incident-action-authorization
L224:     https://probityai.github.io/agent-evidence-vectors/predicate/v1/
L225:       revocation-sweep
L226:     https://probityai.github.io/agent-evidence-vectors/predicate/v1/
L227:       re-enable-decision
L228:     https://probityai.github.io/agent-evidence-vectors/predicate/v1/
L229:       joint-authority
L230:     https://probityai.github.io/agent-evidence-vectors/predicate/v1/
L231:       revocation-boundary
L232: 【138†¶】
L233: 
L234: Each URI is the common prefix on the first line followed directly by the type name on the second, with no space or line break.【139†¶】
L235: ### 【41†5.1.】 【42†R1: Incident action authorization】
L236: 
L237: An R1 records who authorized one incident response action, which role each named party held, on what kind of grant the authorizer acted, and whether the authority was committed before the action ran.【140†¶】
L238: 
L239: The subject is the operation authorized: one or more members, each the SHA-256 of the operation's declared description.【141†¶】
L240: 
L241: The predicate carries the common members and:【142†¶】
L242: 
L243: action:
L244: `functions`, a non-empty sorted list of `response_function` values (`monitoring_increase`, `restriction`, `isolation`, `pause`, `remediation`, `restoration`); `targets`, a non-empty list of `{id}` naming the agents, tools, routes or credentials acted on; and `inducedEffects`, which is one of `{"declared": "listed", "items": [...]}`, `{"declared": "none_observed", "observation": {"sha256": ...}}` or `{"declared": "unknown"}`.
L245: A credential revocation is recorded as `restriction`, and its reach as an R2.【143†¶】
L246: 
L247: parties:
L248: 
L249: 
L250: A non-empty list of `{id, roles, authorityBasis?, independenceBasis?}`. `roles` is a non-empty sorted list drawn from `advised`, `authorized`, `executed` and `accountable`. One party MAY hold several roles. `authorityBasis` is one of `role_grant`, `policy_preauthorized`, `contract_third_party`, `executive_approval` and `unknown`, and MUST be present on every party holding `authorized`. `independenceBasis` is an `independence_basis` value.【144†¶】
L251: 
L252: 
L253: authorizedAt, notAfter:
L254: When the authority was given, and when it lapses.【145†¶】
L255: 
L256: 
L257: executedAt:
L258: 
L259: 
L260: Optional. When the action ran.【146†¶】
L261: 
L262: 
L263: intentBinding:
L264: 
L265: 
L266: An `intent_binding` value: `committed_before_execution` or `asserted_after_execution`.【147†¶】
L267: 
L268: 
L269: pause:
L270: 
L271: 
L272: Optional. `{hold, holdProof}`, where `hold` is a `pause_hold` value and `holdProof` is `{sha256}` of the observation that established it.【148†¶】
L273: 
L274: 【149†Table 2】
L275: #  | Rule  | Code
L276: --- | --- | ---
L277: 4  | At least one party holds `authorized`  | `no-authorizer`
L278: 5  | At least one party holds `accountable`  | `no-accountable-party`
L279: 6  | Every party holding `authorized` carries `authorityBasis`  | `authority-basis-missing`
L280: 7  | `authorizedAt` is not after `notAfter`  | `authorization-window-inverted`
L281: 8  | When `intentBinding` is `committed_before_execution` and `executedAt` is present, `executedAt` is not before `authorizedAt`  | `intent-not-committed-before`
L282: 9  | When `executedAt` is present, it is not after `notAfter`  | `authorization-expired`
L283: 10  | `inducedEffects` declared `none_observed` carries `observation`  | `induced-effects-unobserved`
L284: A record passing every rule is accepted as `authorization-recorded`. A reader MUST NOT read an absent `authorityBasis` as `role_grant`; the value for not knowing is `unknown`.【150†¶】
L285: ### 【43†5.2.】 【44†R2: Revocation sweep】
L286: 
L287: An R2 records which credentials of a declared population were revoked during an incident, which were not, and how far the producer claims the sweep reaches.【151†¶】
L288: 
L289: The subject is the population manifest: one member, the SHA-256 of the list of credential identifiers the sweep was run over. Identifiers are opaque names; they MUST NOT be secrets, hashes of secrets or key fingerprints.【152†¶】
L290: The predicate carries the common members, `predecessors` (at least one R1, the authorization of the sweep), and:【153†¶】
L291: 
L292: population:
L293: 
L294: 
L295: `credentials`, a non-empty, sorted, duplicate-free list of identifiers.【154†¶】
L296: 
L297: 
L298: partition:
L299: 
L300: 
L301: A list of `{state, credentials}` parts, `state` one of `revoked`, `retained` and `unassessed`.【155†¶】
L302: 
L303: 
L304: revocations:
L305: One entry per revoked credential: `credential`; `revokedAt`; `evidence`, a resource descriptor `{digest, uri?, mediaType?}` of the deny record or policy change; and `relyingParties`, a list of `{id, state}` with `state` a `revocation_state` value (`issued`, `enforced_observed`, `use_after_revocation`, `not_established`).【156†¶】
L306: 
L307: 
L308: coverage:
L309: `claim`, one of `complete_verified`, `issued_after_only`, `partial` and `unknown`; and `issuedAfter`, a time, present when `claim` is `issued_after_only`.【157†¶】
L310: 
L311: 【158†Table 3】
L312: #  | Rule  | Code
L313: --- | --- | ---
L314: 4  | The parts are disjoint and their union equals `population.credentials`  | `denominator-union-mismatch`
L315: 5  | `revocations` names exactly the credentials of the `revoked` part  | `revocation-entries-mismatch`
L316: 6  | `complete_verified` is claimed only when every credential is in the `revoked` part  | `coverage-claim-exceeds-proof`
L317: 7  | `issued_after_only` carries `issuedAfter`  | `coverage-claim-incomplete`
L318: A record passing every rule is accepted as `sweep-recorded`. An honest `partial` or `issued_after_only` sweep is well formed. Whether a relying party admits a system restored under it is that party's policy.【159†¶】
L319: ### 【45†5.3.】 【46†R3: Re-enable decision】
L320: 
L321: An R3 records one decision about whether a stopped or restricted agent system may run again: the outcome, the scope restored, who approved it and on what independence, and, for every kind of evidence incident guidance asks a restart to show, either the digest of what was shown or an explicit statement that it was not addressed.【160†¶】
L322: The subject is the configuration restored: one or more members, each the SHA-256 of a baseline (model weights, harness code, container image, tool configuration).【161†¶】
L323: 
L324: The predicate carries the common members, `predecessors` (at least one record of this document), and:【162†¶】
L325: 
L326: restoration:
L327: `decision`, a `restoration_decision` value (`resume_full`, `resume_staged`, `remain_restricted`, `not_established`); and `restoredScope`, present when `decision` is `resume_staged`: `{agents, tools, routes, credentials}`, each a sorted list of identifiers, at least one non-empty.【163†¶】
L328: 
L329: 
L330: approvers:
L331: 
L332: 
L333: A list of `{id, roles, independenceBasis}`, with `roles` as in R1 and `independenceBasis` an `independence_basis` value (`independent_sources`, `subject_supplied`, `undeclared`).【164†¶】
L334: 
L335: setSufficiency:
L336: 
L337: 
L338: The producer's own `set_sufficiency` judgment of the evidence below: `sufficient`, `insufficient` or `not_assessed`.【165†¶】
L339: 
L340: 
L341: evidence:
L342: An object with exactly the sixteen slots of the table below. Each slot is either a resource descriptor, `{"digest": {"sha256": ...}}` with optional `uri` and `mediaType` as in the in-toto ResourceDescriptor, or `{"notAddressed": "<reason>"}` with a non-empty reason. A slot MAY point at an attestation the producer already emits, including an agent audit record [【86†AUDIT-RECORD】].【166†¶】
L343: 
L344: 【167†Table 4】: 【168†Evidence slots of a re-enable decision】
L345: Slot  | What it holds  | Where guidance asks for it
L346: --- | --- | ---
L347: actorObjective  | the adversary's objective, or confirmation it is not apparent  | SP 800-184 Sec. 2.3.4
L348: persistence  | persistence mechanisms understood, or non-persistence confirmed  | SP 800-184 Sec. 2.3.4

L93: # Authorization Revocation for Long-Running AI Agents: Root-Scoped Quiescence under Delegation and Asynchronous Execution
L94: 
L95: CCS: Security and privacy Access control CCS: Mathematics of computing Distributed computing models
L96: 
L97: Genliang Zhu Affiliation: Accentrust, Vancouver, Canada Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia, USA email: research@accentrust.com and Chu Wang Affiliation: Accentrust, Vancouver, Canada Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, Illinois, USA
L98: © none
L99: ###### Abstract.
L100: Long-running AI agents outlive initiating processes through credentials, delegated tasks, queues, callbacks, reservations, and provider-side operations. Cancellation, process exit, and credential revocation neither close every pre-cut carrier nor distinguish independently authorized shared work.
L101: We define root-scoped authorization quiescence: for each manifested sink, a certificate accounts for every cut-relevant acceptance under the retired root-epoch atom that precedes its local fence and excludes protected acceptance under that atom after the fence, while permitting exact rebind to a current, independently sufficient support.
L102: The root-scoped quiescence protocol linearizes a root cut, fences old-root expansion and protected sinks, represents alternative and conjunctive authority as antichains of minimal sufficient root sets, and composes provider-frontier certificates into a cutset over registered old-root paths. Exact channel-token accounting reconciles transfers; missing or conflicting evidence remains indeterminate.
L103: Under stated assumptions, we prove post-cut issuer non-expansion, support-sound projection, compositional soundness under exact channel conservation, independent-support preservation, merge-order independence, and crash/replay stability. A provider-free late-effect test suite matches 17/17 registered outcomes. Two cancellation-only and one cut-only execution accept the same class of already scheduled late effect; two cut-plus-fence executions, one restart, and one stale-process execution reject it.
L104: A separately implemented checker verifies 17/17 traces and rejects 44/44 consistently rehashed semantic regressions. The certificate establishes root-relative authorization quiescence within its bound manifest and configuration, not global idleness, rollback, or business completion.
L105: ###### Keywords:
L106: 
L107: AI agents, access control, authorization revocation, quiescence, distributed systems, cancellation, effect closure
L108: ## 1. Introduction
L109: Long-running agents routinely outlive the interaction that launched them. A single task can create remote subtasks, durable queue entries, scheduled jobs, webhooks, delegated credentials, reservations, and provider-side operations. Stopping the local process therefore need not stop the task’s authority. Even an acknowledged cancellation can race with a remote completion, and a revoked token can leave a prepared operation or separately delegated credential able to commit.
L110: The operational question is not merely whether a controller sent a stop request. It is whether the retired authority has lost every remaining path to a future protected effect and whether every cut-relevant old-atom frontier crossing is terminally accounted.
L111: Existing interfaces expose observations that are useful but individually insufficient for that conclusion. MCP task cancellation and A2A cancellation are cooperative control transitions rather than proofs that every underlying effect has stopped (【81†Model Context Protocol Contributors, 2026】; 【82†A2A Project, 2026】). OAuth token revocation invalidates a named token at the authorization server, subject to the deployment’s propagation and mediation semantics (【83†Lodderstedt et al., 2013】).

L65: # Heartbeat-Bound Hierarchical Credentials: Cryptographic Revocation for AI Agent Swarms
L66: 
L67: Saurabh Deochake Affiliation: SentinelOne Inc.
L68: Mountain View, USA E-mail saurabh.deochake@sentinelone.com
L69: ###### Abstract
L70: Autonomous AI agents that spawn sub-agent swarms create a safety gap: existing credential revocation mechanisms, OAuth 2.0 introspection, OCSP, and W3C Status Lists, require network connectivity to a central authority, leaving “zombie agents” executing privileged operations for minutes to hours after operator shutdown. We present Heartbeat-Bound Hierarchical Credentials (HBHC), a cryptographic protocol that binds credential validity to periodic parent liveness proofs.
L71: Verifiers enforce freshness using only a cached public key and local clock; no network round-trip is required. When heartbeat generation ceases, all descendant credentials become unusable within a deterministically bounded window $W_{z}\leq W_{\max}+\Delta_{h}+\epsilon$, conditional on bounded clock skew and parent keys held in secure enclaves.
L72: Evaluation at the protocol layer and with real LLM-backed agent swarms (GPT-4o-mini) demonstrates a 90$\times$ reduction in the zombie window over OAuth 2.0, 0.26 ms full authentication in Rust, 18,000+ verifications per second under concurrent HTTP load, and stable per-verification latency from 10 to 10,000 agents.
L73: Real-agent experiments show 0.71% end-to-end overhead on tool calls, zero post-revocation tool calls under prompt injection that bypasses application-layer guardrails, and cascading revocation across a 49-agent four-level hierarchy within the theoretical bound.

L77: ## 1 Introduction
L78: Agentic AI systems [【53†16】, 【54†21】] present novel challenges for human control over autonomous software. AI agents dynamically spawn sub-agent swarms, delegate authority across trust boundaries, and execute multi-step plans that can diverge from operator intent. A single orchestrator may instantiate hundreds of workers, each carrying derived credentials with access to APIs, databases, and production infrastructure.
L79: The resulting credential hierarchy mirrors the agent hierarchy: if a parent agent is compromised, hallucinates, or triggers a safety violation, every descendant credential must be invalidated promptly, even when sub-agents execute asynchronously across distributed infrastructure.
L80: Consider a concrete scenario. An autonomous coding assistant spawns 50 sub-agents to patch a production codebase, each carrying derived credentials with write access to repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and deployment targets. Midway through, the orchestrator hallucinates and begins generating patches that introduce security flaws.
L81: The operator terminates the orchestrator, but the 50 sub-agents dispatched with valid OAuth 2.0 tokens (TTL: 1 hour) continue pushing commits, triggering builds, and deploying compromised code until their tokens expire. As inference speeds increase and agent autonomy deepens, this gap between “operator decides to stop” and “all agents actually stop” becomes a first-order safety concern [【55†1】] that the EU AI Act mandates be addressed for high-risk systems [【56†15】].
L82: We term this the zombie agent problem: sub-agents continuing to exercise valid credentials after their parent has been revoked or shut down. The problem is not hypothetical: the ZombieAgent vulnerability [【57†2】] is a zero-click attack on ChatGPT agents that persists in memory and exfiltrates data invisibly; Gu et al. [【58†20】] show that a single adversarial image can compromise one million multimodal agents exponentially fast through inter-agent memory propagation.
L83: Recent surveys systematize these threats [【59†10】]. Credential lifetime bounds the exposure window at 15–60 minutes for OAuth 2.0 access tokens [【60†29】] and 5–15 minutes for short-lived X.509 certificates. Existing revocation mechanisms all require network connectivity: W3C Bitstring Status Lists [【61†34】] require fetching a bitstring, OCSP [【62†31】] requires contacting a responder, and short-lived certificates require renewal from a CA.
L84: In distributed agent deployments, where control-plane outages, IdP failures, API rate-limiting, or cross-region latency spikes can sever the verifier-to-authority connection, these mechanisms provide no safety guarantees.
L85: We propose Heartbeat-Bound Hierarchical Credentials (HBHC), a cryptographic protocol that provides deterministic agent termination by binding credential validity to ongoing parent liveness proofs. Parent agents periodically generate signed heartbeat commitments; sub-agents incorporate a recent heartbeat into every authentication proof; verifiers check freshness using only local time and the parent’s public key, with no network round-trip.
L86: HBHC leverages hierarchical deterministic key derivation [【63†35】, 【64†13】] so that a valid proof requires both the sub-agent’s private key and a fresh parent heartbeat, a conjunction that neither credential theft nor key forgery can bypass.
